goal: Notice the Park Grass plots and our own schoolyard, build the question board and sketch a first model of what sets the number of plant species.
note: Hook and question board first; the class model starts as "more food, more plants". Adapts Harris 1.1 (short opening reading). Last ten minutes: unit 1 readiness check on bio-biodiversity-math, bio-ecosystem-stability-change and bio-population-carrying-capacity (last used grades 9 and 10). Allergy plans for field days collected privately this week.

goal: Plan field sampling: each student proposes where quadrats go, how many and what to record, then the class agrees one protocol with random placement.
note: Candidate kept: individual and collaborative planning that decides the kind, amount and accuracy of data. Retrieval: alg2-study-design-randomness (random placement). If later (grade 11 taker): random placement taught here with a random-number table in its own terms. First 15 minutes: readiness repair in small groups where day 1 showed gaps (one-lesson reteach counted inside the unit).

goal: Estimate percent cover and tell the schoolyard's common plants apart on quadrat photographs before going outside.
note: Term set: quadrat, transect, percent cover, abundance, species richness. Stinging and blistering plants of the site are shown in photographs today and avoided outdoors. Paper path: printed photographs.

goal: Run the first field count: place quadrats at random in a mown and an unmown site and record species and cover.
note: Field day; clean-up 10 minutes inside the session. No-kit path: supplied quadrat photographs counted in class (partial coverage of CUR-ENV.1; the unit plan names the practical step still owed).
supplies: string and tent pegs for quadrat frames; tape measures; magnifiers; gloves; random-number tables; tally sheets
safety: stinging or blistering plants: shown and avoided before the first count; ticks: long trousers, socks over trouser legs and a tick check after work in grass; bee or plant allergies: identified privately and plans followed; sun and heat: hats and water; hands: gloves; animals: not handled; field work: groups with an adult on school grounds or an approved site; thunder: outdoor work stops; clean-up: 10 minutes

goal: Repeat the count: resample one plot several times and the second site, so the class can see how much a count varies.
note: Field day; clean-up 10 minutes. Retrieval: alg2-sample-estimates-margin. If later: variation shown by repeated sampling of one plot, with no margin formula.
supplies: string and tent pegs for quadrat frames; tape measures; magnifiers; gloves; tally sheets
safety: stinging or blistering plants: shown and avoided before the first count; ticks: long trousers, socks over trouser legs and a tick check after work in grass; bee or plant allergies: identified privately and plans followed; sun and heat: hats and water; hands: gloves; animals: not handled; field work: groups with an adult on school grounds or an approved site; thunder: outdoor work stops; clean-up: 10 minutes

goal: Work out species richness and Simpson's diversity index from the class's own counts.
note: Simpson's index as one minus the sum of squared proportions, no logarithm. Adapts Harris 5.1 (measuring diversity). Deepens HS-LS2-2 (Biology unit 5), named as review: there the data were supplied, here the class collected them.

goal: Practice richness and Simpson's index on new supplied quadrat sets.
note: Short independent set, unscored; answers checked in pairs.

goal: Judge whether the difference between two sites is larger than the spread between repeated quadrats.
note: Sampling variation compared with a between-site difference from the repeated counts of day 5; no statistical test beyond that comparison.

goal: Compare what our counts can show (a correlation) with what a designed experiment can show, using the Park Grass plan of control and treated plots.
note: Nature of science on purpose: investigations use diverse methods (Candidate kept). Retrieval: alg1-correlation-causation (a controlled experiment against a correlation).

goal: Read the Park Grass records of species number against nutrients added and describe the pattern.
note: Retrieval: alg1-scatter-linear-models (species count against nitrogen added). Data card set redrawn from the experiment's published results.

goal: Explain how soil acidity and competition for light, beside the nutrients, set how many species a plot holds.
note: Limed against unlimed plots; tall grasses shading small plants. Adapts Harris 4.1, 4.2 and 4.4 (populations and competition, retrieval of Biology unit 5). Deepens HS-LS2-6 (Biology unit 5), named as review.

goal: Revise the class model of what sets species number and test it against the schoolyard counts and a century of Park Grass change.
note: Model revision point: "more food, more plants" becomes nutrients, acidity and competition. Adapts Harris 3.3 (one framing reading placing the meadow and schoolyard in their biome).

goal: Draft the field sampling report from the class's counts: method, richness and index, the site difference and its uncertainty.
note: Drafts collected for written feedback before day 15.

goal: Predict the species count of a Park Grass plot under a treatment the class has not read and argue the prediction from the records.
note: Argument practice in pairs while the teacher returns written feedback on the drafts.

goal: Revise the field sampling report from the written feedback; the revised report is handed in and scored.
note: End-of-unit product (CUR-ENV.1, CUR-ENV.2), scored after this revision lesson, never on a day a topic is first taught. Every part of each code has its own criterion: planning and carrying out, uncertainty recorded, richness and index, difference judged against variation.

goal: Return to the question board and answer the anchor question with the revised model, then practice explaining an unfamiliar plot record.
note: Question board closed; questions left open are carried to unit 2.

goal: Explain an unseen long-term grassland experiment's records: what the treatments did to species number and why.
note: End-of-unit sitting (CUR-ENV.3), a prompt per part: nutrient, acidity and competition drivers, and why a designed experiment supports a cause. The unseen case is not Park Grass.

goal: Respond once to the scored report and the sitting.
note: Response time for both end days, counted once here. Last ten minutes: unit 2 readiness check on chem-resource-cost-benefit (last used grade 10).

goal: Notice how the Yellow River's sediment fell, build the question board and sketch a first model of why soil washes away.
note: Hook and question board first; the first model blames rain alone. Retrieval: chem-water-earth-materials (water weathers and carries rock). Sensitivity: farming families on the plateau; the unit uses Chinese researchers' own published studies. US History II's Dust Bowl is not reused.

goal: Describe how a soil forms from weathered rock and living things, and read a soil profile layer by layer.
note: Adapts Harris 9.1 (soil profiles). Deepens HS-ESS2-5 (Chemistry unit 3), named as review: the weathered material is now a living soil. Readiness repair (chem-resource-cost-benefit) waits for day 26, where it is used.

goal: Set up a settling jar and test texture by feel on school-garden soil.
note: Bench lab; jars settle overnight. Clean-up 5 minutes. No-kit path: supplied soil test results (partial coverage of CUR-ENV.4).
supplies: clear jars with lids; school-garden soil; water; trays; gloves; eye protection
safety: soil: gloves on, hands washed after, none from roadsides or old building sites (lead); splashes: eye protection on; tests: pH strips only, no strong reagents, no hydrogen peroxide; glass jars: on a tray; clean-up: 5 minutes

goal: Read the settled layers as percent sand, silt and clay, and measure infiltration with a can pressed into the ground.
note: Retrieval: m7-percent-problems (percent of each layer). Infiltration timed outdoors on two surfaces; clean-up 5 minutes.
supplies: settled jars from day 21; tin cans open at both ends; rulers; water; timers; gloves; eye protection
safety: soil: gloves on, hands washed after, none from roadsides or old building sites (lead); splashes: eye protection on; tests: pH strips only, no strong reagents, no hydrogen peroxide; glass jars: on a tray; clean-up: 5 minutes

goal: Test pH by strip and judge organic matter by color and floating material, then relate each property to how soil holds water and nutrients.
note: Adapts Harris 9.2 (soil and plants). No hydrogen peroxide test; organic matter is judged by color and by what floats in the jar.
supplies: pH strips; soil samples; distilled water; cups; trays; gloves; eye protection
safety: soil: gloves on, hands washed after, none from roadsides or old building sites (lead); splashes: eye protection on; tests: pH strips only, no strong reagents, no hydrogen peroxide; glass jars: on a tray; clean-up: 5 minutes

goal: Use the class's soil results to explain which soil would hold water and which would wash away, from its structure.
note: Candidate kept: functions and properties inferred from overall structure (texture and pore space to infiltration). Model revision point: soil now has a structure, not only rain on it.

goal: Explain how rain, slope and land cover combine to erode soil, using the rain-on-slope tool or its table of measured losses.
note: No erosion equation beyond comparing measured losses.

goal: Compare terraces, cover crops, no-till and replanting from erosion and yield data, and name what each costs and earns a farmer.
note: Adapts Harris 9.3 and 9.5. Retrieval: alg1-percent-change-interest (percent change in sediment and yield) and bio-evaluate-impact-solutions (criteria and trade-offs). Readiness repair for chem-resource-cost-benefit where day 18 showed gaps. Bridge (Economics unit 1 comes later, school weeks 17 to 18): the incentive idea named in its own terms, what a practice costs and earns.

goal: Practice percent change in sediment load and yield on new practice records.
note: Short independent set, unscored.

goal: Read the Loess Plateau evidence pack (terraces, check dams, replanting, river dams, rainfall) and judge which practices held the soil.
note: Sensitivity: the people moved from the steepest slopes and the farming families, told through the published accounts of those who ran and lived under the program. Deepens HS-ESS3-2 (Chemistry unit 11), named as review.

goal: Argue in groups how much of the river's change came from land practices and how much from dams and less rain.
note: Candidate kept: competing design solutions evaluated from evidence and principles. Rival causes weighed, each on its own evidence.

goal: Explain what else runs off a field with its soil (fertilizer and pesticides) and where it goes next.
note: Adapts Harris 9.4 (pests and pesticides), the bridge into unit 3's runoff.

goal: Judge a farm practice choice in a region the class has not studied from its soil and erosion data, then close the question board.
note: Transfer practice; the end sitting uses another region.

goal: Relate an unseen soil test set to its formation and water holding, and weigh the rival causes in an unseen erosion and sediment record.
note: End-of-unit sitting (CUR-ENV.4, CUR-ENV.5), a prompt per part: each soil property, its link to formation and to water and nutrient holding, the erosion drivers, a practice judged and a rival cause weighed.

goal: Respond once to the end-of-unit sitting.
note: Response time counted once here. Last ten minutes: unit 3 readiness check on bio-carbon-cycle, chem-human-earth-systems and s7-human-impact-design (last used grade 10).

goal: Notice the Toledo do-not-drink order and the bloom on Lake Erie, build the question board and sketch a first model from field to tap.
note: Hook and question board first. Sensitivity: families who have had unsafe water or rely on wells; Flint is not used. Figures pinned from the city's and the state environmental agency's published reports.

goal: Trace nitrogen and phosphorus through their cycles as stocks and flows.
note: Adapts Harris 3.2. Matter-cycle model returns at watershed scale. First 15 minutes: readiness repair (bio-carbon-cycle, chem-human-earth-systems) where day 33 showed gaps, using carbon as the worked case.

goal: Read a supplied watershed outline and predict where a river's nutrient load comes from.
note: Watershed part-lesson in this course's own terms (the land draining to one point); Earth and Space Science unit 4 owns the map work. Candidate kept: a model used to predict relationships between systems (fields, towns, river, lake).

goal: Explain how extra nutrients grow a bloom and how its decay pulls oxygen out of deep water, from oxygen profiles.
note: Adapts Harris 3.4 (lakes and rivers).

goal: Plot spring phosphorus load against summer bloom size for Lake Erie and describe the relation.
note: Retrieval: alg1-scatter-linear-models. Records from the federal Great Lakes laboratory.

goal: Use the watershed nutrient tool or a stock-and-flow table to predict the bloom if the spring load were cut.
note: Candidate kept: matter conserved in a system (every kilogram of phosphorus in the load is accounted for in the lake, its sediment or its outflow). Deepens HS-ESS3-6 (Chemistry unit 10), named as review.

goal: Test water for nitrate, pH and turbidity with strips and a transparency tube.
note: Bench lab on tap water, rainwater and a teacher-collected pond sample; clean-up 5 minutes. Retrieval: alg2-logarithms (pH as a logarithm). If later: pH read as powers of ten, as Chemistry taught it. Retrieval: s7-human-impact-design (monitoring local water) and its readiness repair.
supplies: nitrate test strips; pH test strips; transparency tube; sample cups; gloves; eye protection
safety: water samples: eye protection, gloves, cuts covered, hands washed after; water tests: strips and a transparency tube only, no liquid or tablet reagents; algal scum or a sewage overflow: never sampled or touched; clean-up: 5 minutes

goal: Sort stream animals into sensitive, somewhat tolerant and tolerant groups from photographs and score the tolerance index.
note: Three groups weighted 3, 2 and 1, as volunteer stream monitors use.

goal: Sample a shallow approved stream: run the water tests and kick-net the animals.

supplies: nitrate test strips; pH test strips; transparency tube; kick net; white trays; sample cups; gloves; eye protection
safety: stream work: shallow, slow water below the knee, with an adult, never after rain; algal scum or a sewage overflow: never sampled or touched; stream water: eye protection, gloves, cuts covered, hands washed after; water tests: strips and a transparency tube only, no liquid or tablet reagents; stream animals: shaded water in white trays, returned where found; ticks: long trousers, socks over trouser legs and a tick check after; thunder: outdoor work stops; clean-up: 10 minutes

goal: Judge the stream's health from the class's tests, the tolerance index and published dissolved oxygen records.
note: Dissolved oxygen from published monitoring records or a loaned electronic meter.

goal: Practice the tolerance index and test readings on new supplied stream records.
note: Short independent set, unscored.

goal: Explain where a town's water comes from: rivers, reservoirs and wells, the water table and flow toward a pumped well.
note: Adapts Harris 7.1 and 7.2. Groundwater part-lesson kept to the water table and flow toward wells. Sensitivity: families on wells.

goal: Explain how diversion drew down the Aral Sea, from satellite images and records.
note: Adapts Harris 7.5 (the Aral Sea supply case).

goal: Put drinking water treatment steps in order and find where each can fail.
note: Adapts Harris 7.3 and 7.4. Deepens HS-ESS3-4 (Biology unit 9), named as review.

goal: Explain the Toledo order from field to tap and revise the class model.
note: Model revision point: the bloom and the plant become one system with failure points. Sensitivity: unsafe tap water.

goal: Close the question board and practice on a short unfamiliar river record.
note: The practice record is not the Gulf case of day 50.

goal: Explain the low-oxygen zone off the Mississippi mouth from its monitoring records, and score a stream's test results and animal counts with the tolerance index.
note: End-of-unit sitting (CUR-ENV.6, CUR-ENV.7), a prompt per part: nutrient path, bloom, low oxygen; tests, index, supply and treatment. The class's stream record is reused unscored as one item's context.

goal: Respond once to the end-of-unit sitting.
note: Response time counted once here.

goal: Course-level check 1, part 1: judge an unseen pair of sites' quadrat counts against sampling variation and explain an unseen long-term field experiment's records.
note: Samples units 1 and 2 only; unit 3, assessed at its end two days before, returns in check 2. The class's unit 1 field counts reused unscored as one item's context. Unseen cases differ from days 16 and 17.

goal: Course-level check 1, part 2: relate an unseen soil test set to its formation and judge its erosion record.
note: A data set with constructed responses; the region differs from days 31 and 32.

goal: Respond once to course-level check 1.
note: First 40 minutes: response. Last ten minutes: unit 4 readiness check on chem-climate-forecast and chem-carbon-cycle-quantitative (last used grade 10).

goal: Notice Britain's coal share falling to nothing between 2012 and 2024, build the question board and sketch a first model of a national grid.
note: Hook and question board first. Sensitivity: coal communities and lost jobs; students whose families work in fuel industries; no student is asked to declare a political view. Figures pinned from the government's energy statistics and its notice of the Ratcliffe-on-Soar closing.

goal: Trace energy from fuel to electricity and the losses on the way, as flows into, out of and within a power station.
note: Adapts Harris 11.1 and 1.3 (sustainability). Retrieval: chem-energy-device-design. Candidate kept: energy and matter flows into, out of and within a system. First 15 minutes: readiness repair (chem-climate-forecast, chem-carbon-cycle-quantitative) where day 54 showed gaps.

goal: Measure a small solar cell's output as the light on it changes.
note: Bench lab, low voltage only; clean-up 5 minutes. No-kit path: supplied solar cell readings.
supplies: small solar cells; multimeters; clamp lamps; rulers
safety: solar cell and multimeter: low voltage only, never mains wiring; lamps: switched off and cooled before moving, kept away from water; clean-up: 5 minutes

goal: Compare coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, wind and solar per unit of electricity: life-cycle emissions, land and water.
note: Adapts Harris 11.2 and 11.3. Retrieval: geo-modeling-objects-density (per unit, units tracked). Published life-cycle numbers read, none built.

goal: Compare reliability and cost: capacity factor, intermittency, storage and electricity prices as data.
note: Adapts Harris 11.4 (alternative fuels; its chapter attributions read CC BY). Retrieval: chem-resource-cost-benefit (resource choices weighed by cost and benefit). Bridge (Economics unit 2 comes later, school weeks 18 to 20): prices read as data, set by supply and demand, nothing more. Deepens HS-ESS3-2 (Chemistry unit 11), named as review.

goal: Practice per-unit comparisons of energy sources on a new supplied data set.
note: Short independent set, unscored.

goal: Read the measured records first (carbon dioxide in air, the temperature record, power's share of emissions), then say what they show about burning coal.
note: Evidence meets belief (climate change): the records come first and the day teaches plainly and respectfully what they show. Adapts Harris 10.4 as retrieval of chem-climate-forecast and chem-carbon-cycle-quantitative, not taught again. Deepens HS-ESS3-5 (Chemistry unit 9), named as review.

goal: Read Britain's grid records by year (each fuel's share and the emissions) and work out the percent changes.
note: Retrieval: alg1-percent-change-interest.

goal: List the rival explanations for the fall in coal: a carbon price floor from 2013, gas prices, European plant rules, wind and solar growth and falling demand.
note: Adapts Harris 13.1 (prices and external costs). Bridge (Economics unit 4 comes later, school weeks 22 to 23): the carbon price explained as a cost added to pollution. Nature of science: weighing alternative explanations (Candidate kept).

goal: Weigh each rival explanation against the timing in the records and argue which drove the change most.
note: Candidate kept: claims, evidence and reasoning behind an accepted explanation evaluated. Government unit 8 runs alongside (weeks 13 to 15): the policy is judged by its records only, and the argument over it waits for Government.

goal: Run the electricity mix tool to test what a different mix would have done to emissions.
note: Paper path: a yearly table of shares and emissions.

goal: Write the explanation of how Britain stopped burning coal for power, with the rival causes weighed.
note: Sensitivity: former coal communities' own published accounts read beside the records; jobs lost are named, not judged. Deepens HS-ESS3-4 (Biology unit 9), named as review.

goal: Read a second country's short grid record and close the question board.
note: Transfer practice; the end sitting uses another country.

goal: Explain an unseen country's grid record against rival causes and compare energy sources from a supplied data set.
note: End-of-unit sitting (CUR-ENV.8, CUR-ENV.9), a prompt per part: each comparison measure, the change in mix and emissions, and each rival cause weighed.

goal: Respond once to the end-of-unit sitting.
note: Response time counted once here. Last ten minutes: unit 5 readiness check on s7-resource-distribution (last used grade 10) and, for a grade 11 taker, bio-sources-of-variation (last used grade 9).

goal: Notice the abandoned uranium mines on the Navajo Nation and the Nation's own work on them, build the question board and sketch a first pathway model.
note: Hook and question board first. Fresh sensitivity read of the unit before its unit plan (later.csv L68).

goal: Trace a mined material from extraction and milling to waste rock and tailings, decades past closure.
note: Retrieval: chem-nuclear-processes (decay and half-life, qualitative). Readiness repair (s7-resource-distribution) where day 69 showed gaps. Adapts Harris 1.5 (environmental justice and Indigenous struggles) after its sensitivity read. Deepens HS-ESS3-2 (Chemistry unit 11), named as review.

goal: Explain how contaminants move from mine waste into air, water, soil and homes, and how groundwater flows toward wells.
note: Groundwater part-lesson kept to the water table and flow toward wells (Earth and Space Science unit 4 owns flow). Sensitivity: homes built with waste rock described from the Nation's and federal agencies' public pages.

goal: Model leaching with colored drink powder washed through sand, and measure how far and how fast it moves.
note: Bench lab; no ore, rock or mine waste. Clean-up 5 minutes. No-kit path: a recorded run.

safety: leaching model: colored drink powder and sand only, eye protection on, spills wiped at once; ore, rock or mine waste: never in class; clean-up: 5 minutes

goal: Judge an exposure from amount, pathway and time, working dose from concentration, intake and body mass against the drinking-water limit.

goal: Read dose-response and biomagnification from published data and match each pathway to its harm.
note: Adapts Harris 6.3. Uranium in water acts mainly as a chemical that damages the kidneys; radon in air is the radiation route and raises lung cancer risk; DNA change belongs to the radiation route only (bio-sources-of-variation retrieval). Deepens HS-LS3-2 (Biology unit 6), named as review.

goal: Compare risk among the exposed with risk among the unexposed, and tell a cause from a correlation in health studies.
note: Retrieval: geo-conditional-independence. Candidate kept: empirical evidence needed to tell cause from correlation; Candidate kept: scientific literature adapted for class read for its central conclusions (the Navajo Birth Cohort Study's community reports). Sensitivity: illness; no class collection of health information.

goal: Explain who decides the cleanup and how: the Navajo Nation as a government, its research board, federal agencies, and the choices of cost, time and the wishes of the people affected.

The 1979 Church Rock tailings spill from the Nation's own accounts. Science says what can happen; values and law decide what should.

goal: Follow a town's waste: reduced, reused, recycled or landfilled, how a landfill is lined and watched, and where electronic waste ends.
note: Adapts Harris 12.1, 12.2 and 12.4 (chapter 12 attributions read CC BY).

goal: Practice dose and exposure readings on new supplied cases.
note: Short independent set, unscored.

goal: Draft the evidence report on one mine's pathway and risk from the unit's evidence pack.

goal: Test cleanup choices with the contaminant pathway tool or a dose table, weighing cost, time and the wishes of the people affected.
note: Paper path: a pathway diagram and dose table. Written feedback returned at the end.

goal: Revise the evidence report from the written feedback; the revised report is handed in and scored.
note: End-of-unit product (CUR-ENV.10, CUR-ENV.11), scored after this revision lesson, a criterion per part of each code. Due school day 82, off ELA 12's check days 83 to 85.

goal: Close the question board and practice tracing a pathway in a short unfamiliar case.
note: The practice case is not the transfer case of day 84.

goal: Trace the pathway and judge the risk in an unseen hazardous-waste case.

goal: Respond once to the scored report and the sitting.
note: Response time for both end days, counted once here. Last ten minutes: unit 6 readiness check on s7-population-consumption and bio-energy-pyramids (last used grades 9 and 10).
